631.title: As much as you can
631.hook: be mindful of Allah as much as you are able (64:16)
631.howItsDone: Islamic law builds many concessions on this principle: the sick may pray sitting or lying down, travelers shorten prayers, and those unable to fast make up the days or feed the poor; many Muslims also favor small, steady devotions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qalb, the heart God guides through loss, and Umm Salama's words. Your line was he guides the heart through it.

New Year's resolutions have a famous shelf life. Up at five every day. Gym seven days a week. A book a week. Never eat sugar again. By February, many are gone, and often the person feels worse than if they'd never started. The plan was too big to carry, so they carried none of it. Near its end, Surah At-Taghabun gives a command that sounds almost like a correction to that habit. It asks for everything, then adds four words.

Verse sixteen. Pickthall: "So keep your duty to Allah as best ye can". In Arabic: fattaqu llaha mastata'tum. Be mindful of God, as much as you are able. The verse goes on: listen, and obey, and spend; that's better for yourselves. Commentators set it beside a verse in Surah Al 'Imran: be mindful of God as he deserves to be. Some early scholars thought this verse eased the earlier one. Many others said the two explain each other: God deserves complete mindfulness, and what he asks of each person is that, within their real capacity. Surah Al-Baqarah states the principle. Pickthall: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The hadith makes it practical. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet ﷺ saying: when I forbid you something, avoid it; when I command you something, do of it as much as you can. Another report in Bukhari says the deeds most loved by God are the ones done consistently, even if small. Put those together and you get a very different plan from a New Year's resolution. Not everything at once, then nothing. As much as you can, then keep going. The sick person prays sitting; if not sitting, lying down. The traveler shortens. The one who can't fast makes it up later or feeds the poor. Islamic law is full of these adjustments, and they all stand on this phrase. As much as you can isn't an excuse for doing less. It's the measure that lets you keep doing it.
screen: `MASTATA'TUM: AS FAR AS YOU ARE ABLE.` · `NO SOUL TASKED BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · `DO OF IT AS MUCH AS YOU CAN.` · `SMALL AND CONSTANT.`

segments.voice: Think of one good intention you've let fall because it was too big: daily prayer, exercise, reading, calling home. Shrink it to a size you could truly do every day, even on a bad day: five minutes, one page, one call a week. Picture doing that small version tomorrow, and the day after, and let your breath be easy, just as much as it is.
Istata'a: to have the capacity, the ability behind Surah At-Taghabun's command to be mindful of God as much as you are able. Today's word.
Your line: done consistently, even if small. Small and steady outlasts big and brief. Day six hundred thirty-one.

632.title: Parting with kindness
632.hook: even divorce comes with limits, a waiting period and kindness (65:1–2)
632.howItsDone: In Islamic law divorce is permitted but hedged with rules: a waiting period ('iddah) during which, in a revocable divorce, the wife normally stays in the home, the option of reconciliation, witnesses, and the instruction that a couple either stay together or part bi-ma'ruf, in kindness. The schools of law differ on details.

segments.voice: Yesterday: istata'a, capacity, and being mindful of God as much as you are able. Your line was done consistently, even if small.

Most endings are messy. A friendship goes quiet. A job ends with a badge handed back at a desk. A marriage ends with lawyers, or silence, or a slammed door. When things fall apart, manners tend to go first. Now open the sixty-fifth surah of the Qur'an. Its name is at-Talaq, divorce. A whole chapter named for an ending, and the first thing it does is slow everything down. Count the days. Don't push anyone out of the house. Bring witnesses. Be kind on the way out the door.

The surah opens by speaking to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and through him to everyone. When you divorce, it says, do it with regard to the waiting period, the 'iddah, and count it carefully. During that time, don't turn the women out of their houses, and they shouldn't leave, except in a case of open indecency. Then a phrase the Qur'an uses elsewhere too: these are the limits of Allah, the hudud, and whoever oversteps them has wronged his own soul. Verse one ends with a quieter line: you don't know, perhaps Allah will bring about something new after this. The waiting period isn't only paperwork. It's a pause. Two people under one roof, still, with time to cool down, and maybe to change their minds. Verse two says what happens when the waiting is over. Either keep them in kindness, or part from them in kindness. The Arabic is bi-ma'ruf: in the way that's recognized as right, decent, fair. Both doors, staying and leaving, carry the same word. And bring two just witnesses, so nobody can later rewrite what happened. The schools of Islamic law work out the details differently: how the waiting is counted, whether the witnesses are required. But the shape is shared. Even the end of a marriage has limits. Even a parting has manners. The Qur'an doesn't pretend divorce never happens. When it does, the one walking away still owes the other decency.

Pick one thing that's ending, big or small: a conversation you keep cutting off, a group chat you've been ghosting, a project that's done. Picture the ending you'd be glad to have given: a clear word, no slammed door, nothing taken that isn't yours. If an ending in your life was hard, let it be hard, and just notice what kindness would have looked like.
Ma'ruf: what's recognized as right and decent, the word Surah At-Talaq uses for how a marriage should both continue and end. Today's word.
Your line: part with kindness. Even an ending can be decent, and kind. Until next time.

633.title: A way out
633.hook: whoever is mindful of Allah, He makes a way out and provides from where he never expects (65:2–3)
633.howItsDone: Some Muslims memorize 65:2–3 and recite it in times of debt, illness or family trouble, alongside the promise that whoever trusts in Allah, He is enough for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'ruf, from the surah named divorce. Your line was part with kindness.

Some problems have walls on every side. The rent and the paycheck don't meet. The diagnosis has no good option. The family fight has gone on so long nobody remembers how it started. The math gets run again at two in the morning, and every road ends in the same brick. In exactly that spot, some Muslims reach for one line from the Qur'an. It isn't in a chapter about miracles or battles. It sits in the middle of yesterday's surah, between the rules for divorce.

Surah at-Talaq, verses two and three. Pickthall: "And whosoever keepeth his duty to Allah, Allah will appoint a way out for him, And will provide for him from (a quarter) whence he hath no expectation." Keeping your duty is Pickthall's phrase for taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, living as someone who knows they're seen. The way out is one Arabic word, makhraj, from the root for going out. Not a cure for every problem. An exit. The second promise is stranger: provision from where you never expected. Not from the road you were staring at. From somewhere off the map. Then: whoever puts their trust in Allah, He is enough for them. Now notice where this sits. The verses around it are about the waiting period, the house, the witnesses, the money owed when a marriage ends. Some commentators read the placement as deliberate. Divorce is a place where people can feel trapped: by money, by children, by fear of being alone. And right there, in the middle of the rules, the Qur'an breaks in with hope. It doesn't promise the exit you wanted. It doesn't say when. It says the walls are not the whole story. Some Muslims memorize these two verses and repeat them when a problem has no visible door, not as a trick to make it vanish, but as a way to keep doing the right thing while they wait for the door they can't see yet.
screen: `TAQWA: LIVING AS ONE WHO IS SEEN.`
`HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE RULES.`

Picture it as a room where you've been staring at the same wall, and let your attention drift to the corners you haven't looked at. If you pray, hold the verse there: a way out, from where you never expected; if not, just breathe with the problem without pushing on it.
Makhraj, an exit, promised in 65:2 to whoever keeps their duty to Allah, with provision from where they never expected. Today's word.
Your line: a way out comes. Sometimes from a corner you weren't watching. Six hundred thirty-three days in.

634.title: Sincere repentance
634.hook: turn to Allah in sincere repentance (66:8)
634.howItsDone: Muslims repent (tawbah) by stopping a wrong, regretting it and resolving not to return to it, and, when another person was harmed, by making amends; astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness, is a familiar phrase of daily speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday: makhraj, the exit promised in the middle of the divorce rules. Your line was a way out comes.

There's the fake apology. "I'm sorry you feel that way." "Mistakes were made." The sorry that's mostly about getting the conversation over with. And there's the rarer kind, where you can hear that the person has actually stopped, looked at what they did, and turned around. Surah sixty-six, at-Tahrim, has a name for that second kind. It asks the believers for a repentance that is, in its word, nasuh.

Verse eight, in Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Turn unto Allah in sincere repentance!" The Arabic is tawbatan nasuha. Tawbah, repentance, comes from a root that means to return. It's not mainly about feeling bad. It's about turning around and walking home. And one of the names of Allah comes from the same root: at-Tawwab, the One who turns, again and again, toward the one who turns back. Both sides are moving. Nasuh is the hard part. It shares a root with nasihah, sincere advice, the kind a true friend gives. A nasuh repentance has nothing hidden in it, no deal on the side, no plan to do it again on Friday. Scholars such as Imam an-Nawawi set out what that looks like. You stop the wrong thing. You regret it. You resolve not to return to it. And if it hurt another person, there's a fourth step: make it right with them, return what was taken, ask their pardon. A hadith in Ibn Majah puts the heart of it in a few words: regret is repentance. And the verse comes with hope, not a scolding: perhaps your Lord will remit your bad deeds. Not perhaps you'll earn it. Perhaps He will. One more thing: sincere doesn't mean perfect. In the scholarly tradition, someone who truly repents and later slips hasn't made the first repentance fake. They turn back again. The door doesn't lock after the first use.

Let one thing come up, not your whole life, one thing, maybe small: a sharp word, a corner cut. Walk it quietly through the four steps: can I stop, do I regret it, will I not go back, is there someone I owe a repair? If you pray, this is a moment for astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness; if you don't, simply turn toward the better thing.
Sincere repentance. Tawbatan nasuha, a turning back with nothing hidden in it: stop, regret, resolve, and repair what you broke. Today's word.
Your line: turn back sincerely. Sincere, not perfect; you can always turn again. Day six hundred thirty-four, done.

635.title: Asiya and Maryam
635.hook: two women set as examples for all believers: Pharaoh's wife and Maryam (66:11–12)
635.howItsDone: Some Muslims memorize and pray Asiya's words from 66:11, asking for a home near Allah in the Garden, and honor her and Maryam among the best of women, as hadith describe them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sincere repentance, tawbatan nasuha. Your line was turn back sincerely. Today, the same surah ends with two women.

Pharaoh's palace. A husband who tells his people he is their lord most high. A wife with everything a palace can give. And one day she asks for a house. Not a bigger palace. A different house, somewhere else entirely. The last verses of surah at-Tahrim hold up two women as examples, for everyone who believes, men and women alike. One is the wife of Pharaoh. The other is Maryam.

Verse eleven, in Pickthall: "And Allah citeth an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh when she said: My Lord! Build for me a home with Thee in the Garden." It goes on: and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds. The Qur'an never gives her name; Asiya comes from the hadith. She's the same woman who, in surah al-Qasas, looked at a baby taken from the river and said: a comfort for me and for you, don't kill him, he may be of use to us. That baby was Musa. Now look at the order of her prayer. A home with Thee, then in the Garden. Commentators noticed she asks for the neighbor before the house: near You first, then where. There's an Arabic saying for it, al-jar qabl ad-dar, the neighbor before the house. Married to Pharaoh, she asked to live near Someone else. Verse twelve turns to Maryam, daughter of 'Imran: she guarded her chastity, she believed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devout. Maryam, the mother of 'Isa, is the one woman the Qur'an calls by name, readers note, and a whole surah carries her name. A hadith in Bukhari says that among women, Maryam and Asiya reached perfection. So the surah ends with one woman inside a tyrant's house and one woman alone, both held up for every believer to learn from. One had a husband who opposed her faith; the other had no husband at all. The surah holds up the faith of each.

If you pray, say her words from the verse slowly, once or a few times: my Lord, build for me a home with Thee in the Garden. If you don't, think of the place you feel most yourself, and notice what makes it home: the walls, or who is near. Let the house fade and the nearness stay.
Asiya. Pharaoh's wife, who asked for a home near Allah before anywhere else, one of two examples, says 66:11–12, for all believers. Today's word.
Your line: a house near you. Nearness first, then the house itself. See you soon.

636.title: The surah before sleep
636.hook: the Prophet ﷺ recited al-Mulk before sleeping, and it intercedes for its reader (Tirmidhi)
636.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite surah al-Mulk (also called Tabarak) every night before sleeping, following hadith that the Prophet did so and that this thirty-verse surah intercedes for its reader; children often learn it by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asiya, who asked for a home near God before the house. Your line was a house near you. Today a new surah begins, one people keep by the bed.

What's the last thing you see before you sleep? For a lot of people it's a phone: one more video, one more scroll, blue light on the ceiling. In many Muslim homes there's an older habit for the last minutes of the day. A short chapter, thirty verses, about five or ten minutes read aloud. Children learn it early. Grandparents say it from memory in the dark. It's surah sixty-seven, al-Mulk, the Sovereignty.

It begins, in Pickthall: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things." Al-mulk: the dominion, the kingship over everything. The first word, tabaraka, blessed, is why many people simply call the surah Tabarak. Two hadith in at-Tirmidhi's collection explain the bedtime habit. In one, a companion reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would not sleep until he had recited two surahs: as-Sajdah, and Tabarak, al-Mulk. In the other, the Prophet says a surah of the Qur'an, thirty verses long, interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and he names it: Tabarak alladhi biyadihi al-mulk. To intercede is to speak up for someone, the way a friend might stand beside you in a hard meeting and say, I know this person. In the hadith, a surah does the speaking. Other narrations call al-Mulk a protector, and many Muslims understand it as a shield for its reader in the grave. Scholars discuss how strong each narration is; the habit of reading it at night is very widely kept. And look at what the surah holds, because we'll spend three more days inside it. Death and life. The sky, looked at again and again. The earth made easy to walk on. Birds held up in the air. It's a surah about being held. Maybe that's why it suits the moment a person lets go of the day and can't hold anything themselves.

Say the first verse, or hear it in your head: blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty. Notice your own hands and what they've been holding today, and let them rest open on your knees. Many keep all thirty verses for the last minutes before sleep, in Arabic or in any translation.
Al-Mulk. The Sovereignty, surah sixty-seven, thirty verses the Prophet read before sleeping, which a hadith says interceded for its reader. Today's word.
Your line: it intercedes. A surah that speaks up for its reader. Rest well tonight.

637.title: Death and life, to test
637.hook: He created death and life to test which of you is best in deed (67:2)
637.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 67:2 to say that what matters before Allah is the quality of a deed, done sincerely and correctly, rather than its quantity; it is also read nightly by those who keep the habit of reciting al-Mulk.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Mulk, the surah before sleep. Your line was it intercedes. Today, its second verse, and the end of a week.

Say it out loud: life and death. That's the usual order in English. Birth first, then the end, like a biography, a gravestone, a hospital chart. Now read the second verse of al-Mulk, and something is backwards. The Qur'an says Allah created death and life. Death first. It's not a slip. And in the same breath it tells you why both were made, and the answer isn't about how much you do.

Al-Mulk, verse two, in Pickthall: "Who hath created life and death that He may try you which of you is best in conduct; and He is the Mighty, the Forgiving." Pickthall turns it into the familiar order. The Arabic says al-mawt wa al-hayah: death, then life. Commentators offered reasons. Some say death is named first because it's the thing people forget, and remembering it changes how life gets lived. Others say every person was lifeless, nothing, before they were given life. The Qur'an doesn't say which; it just puts death in front. Then the purpose: to test you, which of you is ahsanu 'amalan. Best in deed. Not most in deed. Not the longest list, the busiest calendar, the most prayers stacked up. Best. An early ascetic who settled in Mecca, al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, is reported to have explained best as the most sincere and the most correct: done for Allah, and done the right way. One without the other isn't best. The verse closes with two names together: the Mighty, the Forgiving. The test is real, and so is the mercy. The one who sets it can't be fooled, and also forgives. Put the verse on an ordinary day. You don't have to do everything. Death comes for everyone, so the question isn't how much time is left. It's what one thing, done today, could be done well, and for the right reason.
screen: `BEST IN DEED, NOT MOST IN DEED.`

segments.voice: Look at today's list, the real one in your head, and pick one ordinary item: a meal, a reply, a chore, a prayer. Ask two questions: why am I doing it, and how would it look done well? Picture doing it that way, start to finish, with nothing rushed.
Ahsanu 'amalan. Best in deed, not most: in 67:2 Allah creates death, then life, to test which of you is most sincere and most correct. Today's word.
Your line: best in deed. The week ran from small and steady, through kindness, a way out, turning back and a house near you, to the surah before sleep. Another week behind you.

chat.says: If life is a test, shouldn't I just cram in as many good deeds as possible?
options: Al-Mulk asks who is best in deed, not most: sincere, and done the right way.
Yes; the verse says the test goes to whoever does the greatest number of deeds.
No; the verse says to wait until old age, when the real test begins.
